_readme: The FUTURE run of Chapter 2 of the Theory reference. Six articles, authored against DESIGN-THEORY.md section 2 (the article schema), section 5 (the writing standard) and section 6 (the quantity targets), and matched to the voice, depth and block usage of content/ch2-tenses.json.

WHY THIS FILE EXISTS. Before it, the whole Theory reference contained not one article about the future in any form. The practice Path teaches will, going to, the present continuous for the future, the present simple for timetables, the future continuous, the future perfect, the future-form choice and the no-will-after-when rule. A reader who read Theory first and then walked the Path met eight practice points the reference had never mentioned.

CHAPTER ID and SEQUENCE INDEX. chapter_id is thc_02, matching ch2-tenses.json. sequence_index runs 34..39 on the brief's instruction that the two past-perfect articles take the slots immediately after the existing eleven (21..31 authored, 32..33 past perfect). Both fields are provisional in exactly the way ch2-tenses.json declares them provisional; the build agent re-bases them once the eight-chapter split is fixed, and nothing else in this file depends on them.

THREE DECLARED DEVIATIONS FROM DESIGN-THEORY.md section 1.5. (1) Section 1.5 gives the future two articles, th_the_futures (paradigm, I14-I23, I26) and th_future_choice (comparison, I24, I25). One paradigm article cannot carry will, going to, the two present forms doing future work, the future continuous and the future perfect and still obey section 2.3's 350-prose-word cap or section 6.4's one-question test. The run is therefore split into six. th_the_futures is KEPT, with its id and its kind unchanged, because four articles in three already-authored chapters link to it (ch2-tenses.json x3, ch3-modals.json x1, ch5-conditionals.json x2); it becomes the all-at-once table it was always meant to be, and the four teaching articles feed it. (2) th_the_futures is kind: paradigm, and section 2.5 restricts a paradigm article to parts 2, 3 and 11. It additionally carries a variation block and a false_rule block, because it is the only article that owns I23 (shall), and section 5's W32 and section 2.4.12 forbid resolving a variation silently to keep an article tidy. (3) th_future_choice is kind: comparison, and section 2.5's comparison order drops part 7 (exceptions). It carries one exceptions block anyway, because section 1.5's own chapter note requires the no-will-after-when rule to ship WITH its exception, and the exception needs the A/B/C, frequency and verdict labelling that only that block provides.

AREAS OWNED HERE: I14, I15, I16, I17, I18, I19, I20, I21, I22, I23, I24, I25, I26. All thirteen. No area is claimed twice, and none of them is claimed anywhere in ch2-tenses.json or in any other authored chapter.

VARIATION POINTS CLAIMED: TH-R1 section 5 row 6 (shall), in th_the_futures, which owns I23. MYTHS CLAIMED: TH-R4 section 8.3 row 8 (shall is the correct future for I and we), in th_the_futures; row 19 (will is the future tense and going to is informal), in th_future_choice. ch2-tenses.json already claims rows 17 and 18 and variation row 1.

PARADIGMS. Every positive, negative and question pattern in this file is copied from docs/source-material/oxford-tense-forms.txt, rows 'future simple', 'future continuous', 'future perfect' and 'future perfect continuous', and then re-expressed with the two model verbs paint and write that PAR-1 requires. The source example sentences are not reused; every example sentence here is authored fresh in the house world.

related_points[] ids are taken from the closed 154 in staging-grammar/DESIGN.md section 4.2, unit u04: gr_future_will, gr_future_going_to, gr_future_pres_cont, gr_future_pres_simple, gr_future_choice, gr_future_time_clause, gr_future_continuous, gr_future_perfect. All eight are linked, and none is invented. Error codes come from the 53-slug closed enum in section 2.8; the two future-specific slugs, future_will_in_time_clause and future_evidence_vs_intention, are both used.

TERM LEDGER. No article here introduces a term, so terms_introduced is empty in all six. TERM-1 was checked against ledger positions: nothing later than position 54 is used anywhere in this file, which rules out semi-modal, conditional, infinitive, embedded question and question word. The no-will-after-when exception is therefore written as 'a question folded inside a longer sentence', not as an embedded question.

articles.title: Deciding now, and saying what you expect

article_json.one_line: This is the form for a decision you make as you speak, and for what you think happens later.
article_json.short_answer: Use *will* and the base form. *I'll ring the depot.* It fits a decision made now and a guess about later.

body.text: *Will* settles something at the moment you speak
You have not decided yet. Then you decide, and the decision comes out of your mouth in the same breath. *Will* is the form that carries it.
It does the same job for a guess. Nothing in front of you proves it, so you say what you think, and *will* marks it as your view.
Build it from *will* and the base form

body.caption: *Will* never changes shape, whoever the subject is.
body.form_line: *will* plus the base form of the main verb

rows.note: No ending on *will*, and none on the verb after it.

sub_tables.caption: A short answer repeats *will* and stops there.
Two ways to shorten the negative, and both are correct.

examples.text: I'll paint the back gate at the weekend.
examples.gloss: The speaker settles it while speaking.

examples.text: The council will write to every household on the route.
They won't paint the railings until the frost goes.
examples.gloss: The work waits for warmer weather.

examples.text: Will she write the report herself?
examples.gloss: The question is who does the writing.

notes: *He'll* is *he will*. The base form after it is the clue.
Never *Yes, I'll.* A short answer cannot end on a short form.
*'ll not* is heard in British English. *Won't* is commoner everywhere.

body.text: The four jobs *will* does

body.caption: Four situations, and none of them was settled in advance.
rows: you think this is what happens
Prices will rise again next winter.
I'll have the figures ready by Friday.
I'll carry that box for you.
footnotes: Not one of these was decided before the sentence started.

body.lead_in: One example per row above, in the same order.

items.text: That bell has gone again. I'll go and check it.
items.gloss: The speaker chooses on the spot.

items.text: Traffic on the Marlow road will get worse after the works.
items.gloss: That is what the speaker expects.

items.text: I'll email the timetable to you tonight.
items.gloss: A promise the listener can hold the speaker to.

items.text: We will refund every ticket bought before Tuesday.
items.gloss: The money goes back to the people who paid.

body.so_what: Each one settles something at the moment of speaking.

body.caption: You decide at this end; the event sits at the other.

body.text: Use *will* when nothing was settled before you spoke
Use *will* when you decide as you speak, or when you say what you think happens later.

body.lead_in: No plan sits behind any of these. The speaker decides or guesses in the moment.

items.text: The hall is cold. I'll turn the heating on.
items.gloss: The speaker acts on what has been noticed.

items.text: Fewer students will apply if the fee goes up.
items.gloss: That is the writer's expectation.

items.text: I'll wait outside the library for you.
items.gloss: The speaker offers to wait.

body.so_what: Nothing was settled before the sentence started.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: The engineer will to check the pump on Monday.
body.right: The engineer will check the pump on Monday.
body.why_it_happens: Most verbs in front of another verb take *to*: *want to check*, *need to check*. *Will* is a helping verb, and a helping verb is followed by the base form on its own.
body.smallest_fix: Take out *to*. After *will*, use the base form: *will check*.

body.wrong: The new timetable will comes into force in April.
body.right: The new timetable will come into force in April.
body.why_it_happens: The subject is one thing, so the *-s* ending feels owed. *Will* has already dealt with the subject, and the verb after it keeps the base form.
body.smallest_fix: Drop the *-s*. Nothing after *will* ever takes an ending.

body.wrong: I will send the form when I will get home.
body.right: I will send the form when I get home.
body.why_it_happens: Both halves are about later, so both halves seem to need *will*. English marks the future once, in the main clause, and leaves the *when* clause in the present form.
body.smallest_fix: Take *will* out of the *when* clause: *when I get home*.

body.label: Two other jobs *will* does that are not about later

items.text: *Will* can guess about this minute rather than about later.
items.example: That'll be the delivery at the door.

items.text: *Will* can say what typically happens.
items.example: The old lift will stick if you press two buttons.

body.heard: *Will* is the future tense, so every *will* in a sentence is about the future.
body.truth: *Will* is a helping verb, not an ending on the verb, and it has two other jobs. *That'll be the postman* guesses about this minute. *The heater will cut out if the door is open* says what typically happens.
body.what_to_do: Read *will* as *I am sure enough to say so*. Most of the time that lands in the future. Sometimes it lands on now.

body.headline: *Will* plus the base form. Decided now, or guessed now.

body.note: Answers are shown. Nothing here is recorded and nothing is marked.

items.prompt: Which one is right? *She will to send the file.* / *She will send the file.*
items.why: *Will* is a helping verb, and a helping verb is followed by the base form.

items.prompt: Why does *I will call you when I will arrive* need changing?
items.answer: Take *will* out of the *when* clause: *when I arrive*.
items.why: English marks the future once, and the *when* clause keeps the present form.

articles.title: Saying what you had already decided

article_json.one_line: This is the form for a plan you already made, and for what the evidence in front of you points to.
article_json.short_answer: Use *am*, *is* or *are* with *going to* and the base form. *We're going to repaint the gates.* The decision came first.

body.text: The decision was made before you spoke
Somebody has already settled this. You are reporting a plan, not making one. That is the whole difference between *going to* and *will*.
It has a second job, and it is not about plans at all. When something in front of you points one way, *going to* says so.
Build it from *be*, *going to* and the base form

body.caption: Only *be* changes. *Going to* and the verb never move.
body.form_line: *am*, *is* or *are* plus *going to* plus the base form

cells: I am not going to paint
you are not going to write
he is not going to paint
we are not going to write
they are not going to paint

sub_tables.caption: A short answer repeats *be* and stops there.
rows: Are you going to paint it?
Is she going to write back?

sub_tables.caption: Two ways to shorten the negative, and both are correct.

examples.text: We're going to paint the community hall in August.
examples.gloss: The date and the job are settled.

examples.text: The trust is going to write to every allotment holder.
They aren't going to paint the upstairs rooms.
examples.gloss: That part has been dropped from the plan.

examples.text: Are you going to write back to the landlord?
examples.gloss: The question is whether a reply is coming.

notes: *He's going to paint* is *he is going to paint*, never *he has*.
In fast speech *going to* runs together and sounds like *gonna*. Do not write it that way.
Never *Yes, I'm.* A short answer cannot end on a short form.

body.text: The two jobs *going to* does

body.caption: A decision made earlier, or evidence you can point at.
rows: We're going to move the depot.
a date already in your head
I'm going to apply in October.
something you can see or hear
Look at that sky. It's going to pour.
Fares are going to rise again.
footnotes: The first two look forward from a decision. The last two look at what is already there.

body.lead_in: One example per row above, in the same order.
body.dimension: what the speaker is going on

items.text: We're going to move the records into the new office.
items.gloss: The move is decided and being organised.

items.text: I'm going to apply for the Ashfield course in October.
items.gloss: The speaker has settled on it.

items.text: The queue is out of the door. We're going to be late.
items.gloss: The speaker can see the reason.

marks.span: The queue is out of the door

items.text: Repairs have stopped, so the bridge is going to close.
items.gloss: The evidence points one way.

body.so_what: The first two came from a decision. The last two came from something visible.

body.caption: The decision is behind you; the event is ahead of you.

body.text: Use *going to* when a decision or evidence came first
Use *going to* when the decision was already made, or when something in front of you points to it.

body.lead_in: No time word decides any of these. The verb carries the meaning alone.

items.text: The Norland site is going to be sold.
items.gloss: The sale has been agreed.

items.text: I'm going to speak to the ward manager.
items.gloss: The speaker settled on this earlier.

items.text: That crack is going to get worse.
items.gloss: You can see the crack, and it is spreading.

body.so_what: Each one rests on something already decided or already visible.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: I have already booked the room. I will run the session on Friday.
body.right: I have already booked the room. I'm going to run the session on Friday.
body.why_it_happens: *Will* was taught as the future, so it comes out for anything ahead. *Will* announces a decision made at this moment, and the booking says the decision came earlier. The two halves then fight.
body.smallest_fix: If the decision came before the sentence, use *going to*.

body.wrong: The tenants going to meet the landlord on Thursday.
body.right: The tenants are going to meet the landlord on Thursday.
body.why_it_happens: *Going* already looks like a verb, so the sentence feels finished without *are*. *Going to* cannot stand on its own; it needs *am*, *is* or *are* in front of it.
body.smallest_fix: Put *am*, *is* or *are* in, matched to the subject.

body.wrong: The two shops is going to close in March.
body.right: The two shops are going to close in March.
body.why_it_happens: A shop closing is one event, so *is* sounds right. The helping verb matches the subject, and the subject here is two shops.
body.smallest_fix: Find the subject, count it, and pick *am*, *is* or *are* from that.

body.label: Two places where *going to* gives way to something else

items.text: With *go* and *come*, the plain *-ing* form is commoner than *going to go*.
items.example: We're going to Sandmouth on Saturday.

items.text: In an *if* clause, a different rule takes over and both *will* and *going to* stay out.
items.example: If the grant comes through, we're going to expand.

body.heard: *Going to* is for plans, and *will* is for everything else in the future.
body.truth: *Going to* has a second job that has nothing to do with planning. *The tide is going to turn* is read off something in front of you, and no plan is involved anywhere in it.
body.what_to_do: Ask two questions. Was the decision already made? Can you point at the evidence? A yes to either one takes *going to*.

body.headline: *Be* plus *going to* plus the base form. Decided earlier, or visible now.

table.caption: One row per situation.
headers: If the decision or evidence is…
rows: a guess with nothing behind it

body.note: Answers are shown. Nothing here is recorded and nothing is marked.

items.prompt: Which one is right? *He going to phone the office.* / *He is going to phone the office.*
items.answer: *He is going to phone the office.*
items.why: *Going to* needs *am*, *is* or *are* in front of it.

items.prompt: Why is *Watch out, the shelf will fall* odd if you can see it tipping?
items.answer: The evidence is in front of you, so write *the shelf is going to fall*.
items.why: Something you can point at takes *going to*, not *will*.

articles.title: Saying what is already in the diary

article_json.also_called: The present continuous and the present simple used for the future
article_json.one_line: These are the two present forms that point forward, for something already fixed with people or already printed in a timetable.
article_json.short_answer: Fixed with other people, write *We're meeting the contractor on Thursday*. Printed in a timetable, write *The ferry leaves at six*.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I talk about something already fixed for later?

body.text: Two present forms that point forward
There is nothing new to build here. You already have both forms. What changes is that the sentence is about later, and the verb stays in the present.
So the sentence needs a time word, or a situation that makes the time obvious to the listener. Without one, it lands on now.
Who fixed it decides which form you use

body.caption: A person agreed it, or a timetable set it. Those take different forms.
rows: a meeting, a visit, an appointment
a train, a flight, a lesson slot
an opening time, a film showing
a shift you have taken on
footnotes: If one person could change it by ringing another person, it is an arrangement.

body.lead_in: One example per row above, in the same order.

items.text: We're meeting the site manager at the Verdon depot on Thursday.
items.gloss: Both sides have agreed the day.

items.text: The last train to Ashfield leaves at eleven twenty.
items.gloss: That is the printed time.

items.text: The clinic opens at half past seven on Mondays.
items.gloss: That is the published opening time.

items.text: I'm covering the front desk on Friday morning.
items.gloss: The speaker has taken the shift on.

body.so_what: A person agreed the first and the last. A timetable settled the middle two.

body.caption: The arrangement is already made; the event sits ahead of now.

body.text: Both forms need a time word, or the sentence means now
*We're meeting the contractor* on its own is happening this minute. Add *on Thursday* and the same three words move forward by a week.
The test is whether a person could change it
Use the *-ing* form for an arrangement with other people. Use the plain present form for a timetable.

body.lead_in: The same speaker, the same week, and only the kind of fixing changes.

items.text: I'm seeing the dentist on Tuesday afternoon.
items.gloss: The surgery gave the speaker that slot.

items.text: The bus to Brackenfield goes every twenty minutes.
items.gloss: That is the service pattern.

items.text: The examiners are visiting the college next term.
items.gloss: The visit has been agreed with the college.

items.text: Term starts on the eighth of September.
items.gloss: That is the date in the college calendar.

body.so_what: The two that a person agreed take the *-ing* form.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: I will meet the site manager on Thursday at ten.
body.right: I'm meeting the site manager on Thursday at ten.
body.why_it_happens: Thursday is ahead, so *will* looks like the marker the sentence needs. *Will* announces a decision made at this moment, and this one was agreed with somebody else days ago.
body.smallest_fix: If it is in the diary and somebody else knows, use *am*, *is* or *are* plus the *-ing* form.

body.wrong: The ferry will leave at six, so be there by half past five.
body.right: The ferry leaves at six, so be there by half past five.
body.why_it_happens: Six o'clock has not happened yet, so a future marker feels owed. A time somebody else printed is treated as a fact about now, and the plain present form states it.
body.smallest_fix: For a timetable, use the plain present form: *leaves*, *opens*, *starts*.

body.wrong: The Sandmouth ferry leave at six on weekdays.
body.right: The Sandmouth ferry leaves at six on weekdays.
body.why_it_happens: The sentence is about later, and future forms take no endings, so the *-s* gets dropped. This is a present form doing a future job, and it keeps every present ending.

body.label: Two cases where the plain present form is the only choice

items.text: A clause starting with *when*, *before* or *after* takes the present form, whatever time it points at.
items.example: Ring me when the delivery arrives.

items.text: A personal plan with no timetable behind it does not take the plain form.
items.example: I'm starting the course in September.

body.heard: The *-ing* form is the now tense, so it cannot talk about the future.
also_known_as: use will for anything in the future
body.truth: It talks about later whenever the arrangement is already made. *We're moving the office in March* is normal English, and nobody is moving anything at the moment of speaking.
body.what_to_do: Keep *now* as the commonest use, and add the second one: something agreed with other people, with the day named in the sentence.

body.headline: Agreed with people, use *-ing*. Set by a timetable, use the plain form.

table.caption: One row per kind of fixing.

body.note: Answers are shown. Nothing here is recorded and nothing is marked.

items.prompt: Which one is right? *The gallery is opening at nine every day.* / *The gallery opens at nine every day.*
items.answer: *The gallery opens at nine every day.*
items.why: Opening times are a timetable, and a timetable takes the plain present form.

items.prompt: Why is *I will see the dentist on Tuesday* odd once the slot is booked?
items.answer: It is agreed with the surgery, so write *I'm seeing the dentist on Tuesday*.
items.why: An arrangement with somebody else takes the *-ing* form.

articles.title: Saying what will be going on, and what will be over

article_json.also_called: The future continuous and the future perfect
article_json.one_line: These two put a second time into the sentence: what is in the middle of happening then, and what is over by then.
article_json.short_answer: *Will be* plus *-ing* for what is under way at that time. *Will have* plus the third form for what is finished by then.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I talk about a point ahead of now?

body.text: Both forms need a second time in the sentence
Plain *will* needs one time: later. These two need a second one. You name a point ahead, and then you say where the event sits against that point.
One of them says the event is in the middle of happening then. The other says it is over by then. That is the whole difference.
Build them from *will be* and *will have*

body.caption: *Will* never changes. What follows it decides which of the two you have.
body.form_line: *will be* plus the *-ing* form, or *will have* plus the third form

sub_tables.caption: *Will* is the same for every subject in both forms.
A short answer repeats *will* and stops there.
rows: Will you be painting on Friday?
Will they have written by then?

examples.text: At nine tomorrow I'll be painting the back stairwell.
examples.gloss: That is what the speaker will have in hand then.

examples.text: The panel will be writing up its findings all week.
examples.gloss: The writing runs across the whole week.

examples.text: By Friday the crew will have painted every landing.
examples.gloss: The job is over before Friday ends.

examples.text: She will have written to all four suppliers by then.
examples.gloss: The letters go out before that point.

notes: Nothing after *will* takes an ending. *Will be*, never *will is*.
After *have*, use the third form: *written*, not *wrote*.
There is a fourth form, *will have been painting*. Recognise it; you do not need to produce it.

body.text: Where the event sits against the point decides the form

body.caption: Ask whether the event runs across the point or stops before it.
rows: At six we'll be crossing the moor.
By six we'll have crossed the moor.
At six we'll leave the depot.
Will you be using the hall on Friday?
footnotes: The last row is not about time at all. It is a way of asking without pressing.

body.lead_in: One example per row above, in the same order.
body.dimension: where the event sits against the point

items.text: At ten on Monday the auditors will be going through the accounts.
items.gloss: They will be in the middle of it then.

items.text: By the end of March the council will have replaced every meter.
items.gloss: The work is finished before April.

items.text: The gates will close at eight.
items.gloss: That is when the closing happens.

items.text: Will you be using the minibus on Saturday?
items.gloss: The speaker wants to know without asking for a favour.

body.so_what: The first runs through the point, the second stops before it, the third starts at it.

body.caption: One point ahead, and two ways of sitting against it.

spec.caption: Across the point, or done before it

body.text: Name the point first, then place the event against it
Use *will be* plus *-ing* for what is under way at that point. Use *will have* plus the third form for what is over.

body.lead_in: The same point in time, and only the position of the event changes.

items.text: This time next week I'll be sitting the speaking test.
items.gloss: The test will be under way then.

items.text: This time next week I'll have sat the speaking test.
items.gloss: It will be behind the speaker by then.

items.text: By 2035 the Norland depot will have closed.
items.gloss: The closure comes before that year ends.

body.so_what: Same week and same test, and only the verb says whether it is over.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: By Friday the team will have wrote the report.
body.right: By Friday the team will have written the report.
body.why_it_happens: *Wrote* is the form you reach for when you talk about the past, and this sentence feels past because the job is done in it. After *have*, English always uses the third form.

body.wrong: By the time the grant will arrive, the site will have closed.
body.right: By the time the grant arrives, the site will have closed.
body.why_it_happens: Both halves point ahead, so both seem to need a future marker. A clause starting with *by the time* keeps the present form, and the main clause carries the future on its own.
body.smallest_fix: Take *will* out after *by the time*: *by the time the grant arrives*.

body.wrong: At this time tomorrow I will be knowing the result.
body.right: At this time tomorrow I will know the result.
body.why_it_happens: *At this time tomorrow* looks like a signal for the *-ing* form, so it drags the verb with it. Knowing is a state, and a state stays out of the *-ing* form whatever the time words say.
body.smallest_fix: Leave the time words alone and use plain *will* with a state verb.

body.label: Two things these forms do that are not about position in time

items.text: The future continuous asks about somebody's plans without pressing them for a favour.
items.example: Will you be driving past the station later?

items.text: *Will have been* plus *-ing* measures a stretch up to a future point.
items.example: By June they will have been running the scheme for a decade.

body.heard: The future continuous is a politer, more advanced way of saying *will*.
also_known_as: will be doing is the formal will
use will be plus -ing to sound higher level
body.truth: It is not a dressed-up *will*. *I'll speak to the landlord* and *I'll be speaking to the landlord* say different things. The first is a decision; the second is something already in hand.
body.what_to_do: Use it when the event runs across a point you have named, or when you are asking about a plan. Never use it to lift the level of a sentence.

body.headline: Under way at that point? *Will be* plus *-ing*. Over by then? *Will have*.

table.caption: One row per position against the point.
headers: If at that point it is…
rows: a state rather than an action

body.note: Answers are shown. Nothing here is recorded and nothing is marked.

items.prompt: Which one is right? *By Friday they will finish the survey.* / *By Friday they will have finished the survey.*
items.answer: *By Friday they will have finished the survey.*
items.why: *By Friday* names a point, and the survey is over before it.

articles.title: The eight ways English talks about the future

article_json.one_line: English puts no future ending on the verb. It has eight ways of pointing forward instead, and this is all of them.
article_json.short_answer: There is no future tense. Use *will*, *going to*, the *-ing* form, the plain present form, or one of four more.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: What are all the ways of talking about the future?

body.text: English marks no future on the verb itself
*Paint* has a past form, *painted*. It has no future form at all. Every row below adds a helping verb or borrows a present form, and each one says something different about how you see the event.
All eight forms, with how often you need them

body.caption: The top four carry almost all of it. The bottom four are mainly for reading.
body.form_line: each row is a different way of pointing forward, not a different tense

notes: Nothing after *will* takes an ending. *Will be*, never *will is*.
Rows five to eight are worth recognising before they are worth producing.
*Going to* is not more informal than *will*. The two say different things.
*Be about to* has no *not* form in ordinary use beyond *is not about to*, which usually means a refusal.

*Was going to* and *would* both carry the future seen from a past moment.

body.why_this_default: Our examples keep *shall* for offers and suggestions and use *will* everywhere else. That is a house choice for this pack, not a rule of English.

body.heard: *Shall* is the correct future for *I* and *we*, and *will* is for everybody else.
body.truth: *Will* is standard for every subject now. *Shall* is alive in two places: offers and suggestions, as in *Shall I carry that?*, and legal writing, as in *The tenant shall keep the property in repair*.
body.what_to_do: Write *will*. Keep *shall* for an offer or a suggestion, where it is the natural word and *will* would sound odd.

articles.title: Which future form does this sentence need?

article_json.one_line: This settles the choice between the four common future forms, so the sentence says how the event came about.
article_json.short_answer: Ask where the future came from. Decided now, *will*. Decided earlier, *going to*. Agreed with people, *-ing*. Set by a timetable, plain form.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I choose between *will*, *going to* and *I'm meeting*?

body.text: All four are correct, and they say different things

*I'll see the surveyor on Thursday* and *I'm seeing the surveyor on Thursday* are both good English. A listener hears a real difference. One sounds like a decision taken this second, and the other sounds like something already in the diary.
So the choice is not about the time. Thursday is Thursday in all four forms. It is about where the future came from.
Where did this future come from?

body.question: Where did this future come from?

options.label: *will*
options.use_it_when: You decide as you speak, or you are guessing with nothing in front of you.
options.example: Fine, I'll collect the parts on my way.

options.label: *going to*
options.use_it_when: The decision was made before you opened your mouth, or the evidence is in front of you.
options.example: We're going to move the office in March.

options.label: the *-ing* form
options.use_it_when: It is arranged with somebody else, and both of you know the day.
options.example: I'm seeing the surveyor on Thursday.

options.label: the plain present form
options.use_it_when: A timetable or a schedule set it, and you are reading the time off.
options.example: The last ferry leaves at eleven.

body.deciding_factor: Ask when the future was settled: as you speak, earlier by you, earlier with somebody else, or by a timetable.
body.trap: You were taught that *will* is the future tense, so it comes out for anything ahead. Three of the four common futures do not use *will* at all.
body.register_note: All four belong in speech and in writing. The choice pays hardest in Speaking Part 2, where a plan and a guess have to sound different.

body.intro: Three questions, in this order. Stop at the first one that answers.

steps.ask: Did a timetable or another person fix this time?

branches.answer: A timetable or a schedule did

verdict.example: The coach leaves at half past six.
verdict.why: You are reading a time off a schedule, so the present form states it.

branches.answer: Another person did, and you both know the day

verdict.example: We're meeting the auditors on Tuesday.
verdict.why: Both sides know, so the arrangement is already a fact about now.

steps.ask: Was the decision made before you started speaking?

verdict.example: I'm going to apply for the Ashfield post.
verdict.why: The decision came first, and *going to* reports it.

steps.ask: Can you point at evidence in front of you?

verdict.example: The sky has gone black. It's going to pour.
verdict.why: Evidence you can point at takes *going to*, not *will*.

branches.answer: No, you are deciding or guessing now

verdict.example: I think the fares will go up again.
verdict.why: A decision made this second, or a guess with nothing behind it.

body.text: Most sentences stop at the first question. The other two exist because a plan and a guess both fail it, and they fail it for different reasons.
*Will* stays out of a *when* clause and an *if* clause
*When the results come out, I'll ring you* holds one *will*, not two. English marks the future once, in the main clause, and the *when* clause keeps the present form.

body.caption: The future is marked once, and never in the *when* part.
rows: When the survey ends, we'll publish it.
If the grant arrives, we'll start in May.
We'll ring as soon as the parts land.
Wait until the light turns green.
footnotes: The main clause keeps *will*. The clause after the joining word gives it up.

body.lead_in: One example per row above, in the same order.

items.text: When the results come out, I'll ring you straight away.
items.gloss: The call follows the results.

items.text: If the grant arrives, the trust will start work in May.
items.gloss: The work depends on the money.

items.text: We'll email you as soon as the parts reach the depot.
items.gloss: The email follows the delivery.

body.so_what: One *will* in each sentence at most, and never after the joining word.

body.label: One place where *will* does belong after *when*

items.text: When *when* starts a question folded inside a longer sentence, *will* stays in.
items.example: Nobody knows when the line will reopen.

items.text: The same holds for *if* used to mean *whether*.
items.example: Ask the office if the hall will be free.

body.text: Choose the future form by where the future came from. Keep *will* out of a *when* clause and an *if* clause.

body.lead_in: The same move, and only the way it was settled changes.

items.text: The clinic is moving to the new health centre in June.
items.gloss: The move is agreed and dated.

items.text: The clinic is going to move once the funding clears.
items.gloss: The decision is made, and the date is not.

items.text: I expect the clinic will move within a year or two.
items.gloss: The speaker is guessing.

body.so_what: Same clinic and same move, and each verb says how firm it is.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: I'll send the photographs when I will get back to the office.
body.right: I'll send the photographs when I get back to the office.
body.why_it_happens: The *when* clause points ahead too, so a second future marker feels owed. English marks the future once and lets the *when* clause sit in the present form.
body.smallest_fix: Delete *will* after *when*. The main clause keeps it.

body.wrong: I have booked the flights. I will travel out on the ninth.
body.right: I have booked the flights. I'm travelling out on the ninth.
body.why_it_happens: The trip is ahead, so *will* looks safe. The booking has already made it an arrangement, and *will* announces something settled at this moment instead.
body.smallest_fix: If it is booked or agreed, use *am*, *is* or *are* plus the *-ing* form.

body.heard: *Will* is the future tense, and *going to* is the informal spoken version of it.
also_known_as: going to is for speaking, will is for writing
body.truth: Neither is more formal. They carry different information. *We will publish the findings* announces a decision; *We are going to publish the findings* reports one already taken. Both belong in an essay.
body.what_to_do: Choose on evidence and timing, not on formality. Use *going to* for a decision already made or evidence you can see, and *will* for a decision made now.
